background.definition: Osteomyelitis is an inflammatory process characterized by bone destruction caused by an infecting organism. In general, osteomyelitis has been categorized as acute, subacute, or chronic. The presentation of each of these categories is based on time of disease onset: acute occurs within 2 weeks, subacute within 1 month to several months, and chronic osteomyelitis occurs after several months.

list.listitem: Approximately 2 per 10,000 persons per year.

In adults, the pathogenic organism(s) is(are) usually associated with etiology or location. Hematogenous osteomyelitis: Staphylococcus aureus. Vertebral osteomyelitis: S. aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Contiguous-focus osteomyelitis without generalized vascular insufficiency: S aureus, gram-negative bacilli, and anaerobic organisms. Contiguous-focus osteomyelitis with generalized vascular insufficiency: multiple organisms are usually isolated from bone, most commonly coagulase-positive and coagulase-negative Staphylococci, Streptococcus spp, Enterococcus spp, gram-negative bacilli, and anaerobic organisms.
S. aureus, group A streptococcus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Kingella kingae are the most common organisms causing osteomyelitis in infants and children.
Osteomyelitis can be caused by hematogenous spread, direct inoculation, or contiguous focus of infection.
Most cases of osteomyelitis in children arise hematogenously, occurring characteristically in the metaphysis of long bones. Hematogenous osteomyelitis in adults usually involves the vertebral bodies.
Penetrating injuries and surgical contamination are the most common causes of direct inoculation osteomyelitis.
Both hematogenous and contiguous-focus osteomyelitis can progress to a chronic condition.

In a study of over 1600 patients with diabetes in a managed care program, 9% developed a foot infection. Risk factors for osteomyelitis in the patients with foot infections were wounds that extended to the bone or joint (relative risk [RR] = 23.1), previous history of a wound prior to enrollment (RR = 2.2), and recurrent or multiple wounds during the study period (RR = 1.9).
Antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated for dental patients with pins, plates, or screws, nor is it routinely indicated for most dental patients with total joint replacements. C

Antibiotic prophylaxis may be considered for higher-risk dental procedures (ie, dental abscess therapy, periodontal treatment, or mouth surgery) performed during the first 2 years following joint replacement, for immunocompromised/immunosuppressed patients, or for patients with certain comorbidities (ie, previous prosthetic joint infections, malnourishment, hemophilia, HIV, diabetes mellitus type I, or malignancy). B
Acute osteomyelitis usually presents with pain, warmth, and tenderness while chronic osteomyelitis presents with a nonhealing ulcer. C
The palpation of bone in the depths of an infected foot ulcer in patients with diabetes suggests presence of underlying osteomyelitis. C

list.listitem: Acute long bone, hematogenous osteomyelitis presents with local pain, warmth, and tenderness while chronic osteomyelitis is often found in the presence of a nonhealing ulcer overlying the involved bone.

Patients may also present with open wound with associated exposed bone, draining sinus tract, deformity, instability, local swelling, and bony tenderness without skin lesion present. In addition, nonspecific pain and low-grade fever may be present.

The palpation of bone in the depths of an infected foot ulcer in patients with diabetes suggests the presence of underlying osteomyelitis. Spinal tenderness to percussion also increases the likelihood of spinal osteomyelitis in patients with back pain.

In a metaanalysis of vertebral osteomyelitis, back pain and fever were the most common presenting symptoms; diabetes was the most common underlying illness, and the urinary tract the most common source. The attributable mortality rate was 6%; relapses and neurologic deficits were common (32% each).

In a metaanalysis of lower extremity osteomyelitis in patients with diabetes, an ulcer larger than 2 cm2 (LR+ 7.2) and a positive probe-to-bone test (LR+ 6.4) were the best clinical findings for predicting osteomyelitis.

The development of osteomyelitis is related to microbial and host factors as listed below. Frequent microorganism in any type of osteomyelitis: S. aureus. Foreign-body-associated infection: coagulase-negative staphylococci or Propionibacterium spp. Common in nosocomial infections: Enterobacteriaceae, P. aeruginosa, Candida spp. Associated with bites, diabetic foot lesions, and decubitus ulcers: Salmonella spp or S. pneumoniae; HIV infection: Bartonella henselae or B. quintana. Human or animal bites: Pasteurella multocida or Eikenella corrodens. Immunocompromised patients: Aspergillus spp, C. albicans, or Mycobacteria spp. Populations in which tuberculosis is prevalent: Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

In patients with diabetes, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) over 70 mm/h was predictive of osteomyelitis (LR+ 11).One study of 48 patients found higher platelet counts in those with osteomyelitis. Using a cutoff of >350 x 109, it was 63% sensitive and 92% specific.

Procalcitonin (PCT) levels at the standard cut-off value of 0.5 ng/ml are more useful for ruling in diagnosis than for exclusion (LR+ 6.48 and LR− 0.37). Use of a lower PCT cut-off value (0.2-0.3 ng/mL) improved the LR+ to 6.66 and the LR− to 0.15.

For late infection following a traumatic fracture (>6 weeks), inflammatory biomarkers were less helpful. Authors of a systematic review found the following positive and negative likelihood ratios for C-reactive protein (CRP; 2.4, 0.3), white blood cell count (1.6, 0.7) and ESR (2.2, 0.7).
In children with septic arthritis, adjacent musculoskeletal infection was predicted by age >4 years, CRP >9 mg/L, platelet count <310, and absolute neutrophil count >7.2.
Deep sinus tract culture accurately predicts the causative organism (using bone culture as the reference standard) especially when two samples are concordant.

Plain films may show soft-tissue swelling, narrowing or widening of joint spaces, bone destruction, and periosteal reaction. Bone destruction is not apparent on plain films until after 10 to 21 days of infection. The American College of Radiology (ACR, 2019) rates radiography as usually appropriate as the initial test for suspected osteomyelitis including suspected osteomyelitis of the foot in patients with diabetes mellitus.

MRI is recommended as the most accurate test for osteomyelitis, including in patients with diabetic foot ulcer, and was 90% sensitive and 79% specific in one review in this population. ACR (2019) recommends MRI as the next imaging study in patients with suspected osteomyelitis for whom initial radiographs are normal or with findings suggestive of osteomyelitis.

Fluorodeoxyglucose PET scanning has the highest diagnostic accuracy for confirming or excluding the diagnosis of chronic osteomyelitis, including in patients with prosthetic implants. However, it is more costly and may be less available than other tests. It may be particularly useful for patients with diabetes.

Authors of a meta-analysis found high accuracy for both MRI and PET scanning for determining osteomyelitis in patients with diabetic foot ulcers with 96.4% sensitivity (95% CI 90.7-98.7) and 83.8 % specificity (76.0-89.5) for MRI, based on 22 studies, and 84.3% sensitivity (52.8-96.3) and 92.8% specificity (75.7-98.2) for PET scans, based on 6 studies.

Spinal tenderness on percussion and the ability to probe to bone in an open wound increase the likelihood of osteomyelitis. Leukocyte count, ESR, and CRP level are often elevated, although normal values do not exclude osteomyelitis.
Cultures from blood or specimens from the bone lesion cultures are used to identify the causative organism.
The preferred initial test is MRI. PET scan is more accurate but also less available and more expensive in most settings.

In suspected acute osteomyelitis, give parenteral antibiotics to treat clinically suspected organisms after cultures have been obtained. In general, antibiotics for the treatment of S. aureus (semisynthetic penicillin or beta-lactam agent if methicillin-sensitive organism is suspected; vancomycin or linezolid if methicillin-resistant organism is suspected) should be given until the results of cultures have been obtained. B

Authors of a Cochrane review, however, concluded that route of antibiotic administration (oral versus parenteral) does not affect the rate of disease remission if the bacteria are sensitive to the antibiotic used. B
Empiric antibiotics for chronic osteomyelitis are usually not recommended. C

In suspected acute osteomyelitis, a parenteral antibiotic regimen is initiated to treat clinically-suspected organisms after cultures have been obtained. In general, antibiotics for the treatment of S. aureus (semisynthetic penicillin or beta-lactam agent if methicillin-sensitive organism is suspected; vancomycin or linezolid if methicillin-resistant organism is suspected) should be given until the results of cultures have been obtained.

In a metaanalysis, there was no difference in treatment success, relapses, or adverse event rates for osteomyelitis comparing fluoroquinolones and beta-lactams. The authors caution against overuse, however, to preserve antimicrobial activity.
As a general rule, antibiotics are administered for 4 to 6 weeks (either parenteral or oral, as appropriate) with antibiotic selection ultimately depending on isolated microorganism.
Authors of a systematic review of 7 randomized trials found that oral treatment was as effective as IV therapy.

Compared with acute osteomyelitis, chronic osteomyelitis in adults is more refractory to therapy and is usually treated with antibiotics and surgical debridement. A systematic review of the treatment of chronic osteomyelitis in adults found only limited data and no difference between oral and parenteral routes of antibiotic administration.
There are no clinical trials of antibiotic selection for osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell disease.
Although acute osteomyelitis is potentially curable with antibiotics alone, chronic osteomyelitis generally cannot be eradicated without surgical treatment.

Authors of a systematic review of case series found that in 239 patients from 24 studies, placing instrumentation during active cervical spine osteomyelitis had good outcomes, with low rates of hardware failure (4.6%) and wound complications (4.0%).
The use of hyperbaric oxygen in the treatment of osteomyelitis had not been adequately studied. A review of case reports and case series found no randomized trials.
Antibiotic therapy for 4 weeks to 6 weeks is generally recommended.
Patients with suspected osteomyelitis may require hospitalization for the initiation of antibiotic therapy and orthopedic consultation to obtain bone specimen for culture.
Prognosis for a good outcome increases following the third month posttreatment, and with every succeeding disease-free month. B The chance of cure after a disease-free year is 95%.
Chronic infection with destruction of bone and adjacent tissue may occur without adequate treatment. C
No clear guidelines are available regarding follow-up tests and additional monitoring. C
Osteomyelitis due to P. aeruginosa is a poor prognostic indicator. B
Ischemia contributes to a poor prognosis in patients with diabetes mellitus and osteomyelitis. B
Osteomyelitis is a major complication associated with a prosthesis.
Removal of the prosthesis is usually required and produces severe functional impairment.

Typical findings in a child with acute hematogenous osteomyelitis include tenderness over the involved bone and a decreased range of motion in adjacent joints, as well as systemic symptoms such as fever, irritability, and lethargy.
A case series of 177 children with acute musculoskeletal infection who underwent MRI found relatively high rates of comorbid osteomyelitis (n = 70), especially among children younger than 2 years.

A retrospective study reported on a cohort of 103 children, most 6 months to 4 years, with spinal infection. Methicillin sensitive staph aureus and Kingella kingae were the most common pathogens, and the lumbar spine (especially L4/L5) was the most common location. Normal white blood cell count (59%) and normal CRP (42%) were common. Blood cultures were rarely positive (8%).
In children with septic arthritis, adjacent musculoskeletal infection was predicted by age >4 years, CRP >9 mg/L, platelet count <310,000 platelets/mL, and absolute neutrophil count >7.2.
